interactive.title: Arrows on the plane
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the coordinate plane with its axes renamed: the real axis across, labelled real (resistance), and the j axis up, labelled j (reactance), the names a later lesson gives them for a circuit. A complex number a + jb is a dot a across and b up, with an arrow from 0 to it, in any of the four quarters. Two arrows have tips you can drag to whole steps. The second arrow is slid, without turning or stretching, so that its tail sits on the first arrow's tip, and a third, bold arrow runs from 0 to where the second one ends: that is the sum. Beside it the across parts and the up parts are added on their own, because moving up does not change how far across you are. A take-away switch turns the second arrow half round first, as multiplying by −1 does, then adds it the same way. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? replays the arrows for it.
interactive.ignores: The dots and arrows only mark the numbers: an arrow means the same number wherever it is slid to, as long as its length and direction stay the same. The tips snap to whole steps so the parts can be counted, but a complex number's parts can be any numbers, fractions included. The words in brackets on the axes name what they hold for a circuit's opposition to AC; a later lesson draws voltages and currents on the same plane.

explain.text:
A complex number has two parts, a real part and a j part, so it needs two directions to draw it: real across and j up, on a flat plane. Adding two complex numbers adds the real parts together and the j parts together, and on the plane that is laying one arrow on the end of the other.

In the last lesson, multiplying by j turned the arrow from 0 to 1 a quarter turn, to point straight up, off the number line. So keep the number line, drawn across, and give the j numbers a line of their own through 0, straight up: j1 one step up, j2 two steps up, −j2 two steps down. This is the plane you plotted points on in The coordinate plane, with its axes renamed. Textbooks call it the [[complex plane]], or an Argand diagram, with the across axis the real axis and the up axis the imaginary axis,[^2] which this course calls the j axis. Say you plot 3 + j2: it sits 3 across and 2 up. −2 − j3 sits 2 to the left and 3 down, so all four quarters of the plane are used. The dot only marks the number; read the number as the arrow from 0 to the dot. Later lessons put this plane to work on a circuit's opposition to AC, which is measured in ohms like resistance.[^3] Textbooks add that its real part is the resistance and its j part the reactance, which is why the axes carry those names in brackets: 6 + j0 lies on the real axis, a pure resistance, and 0 + j4 on the j axis, a pure reactance.[^6]

Say you add (3 + j1) + (1 + j2). The real parts are ordinary numbers, so 3 + 1 = 4. The j parts are counts of j, like the x terms in Linear equations, so one j and two j make three j. A real number and a j number cannot be merged into one part, because one points across and the other up, so the answer keeps both parts: 4 + j3. Lumping every number together, 3 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 7, would land on the real line and lose which way the sum points. The picture shows why. Slide the second arrow, without turning or stretching it, until its tail sits on the first arrow's tip, which is allowed because it still means 1 across and 2 up wherever it is drawn. Following the two arrows, you go 3 across and 1 up, then 1 across and 2 up. Going up does not change how far across you are, and going across does not change how high you are, so the across parts add on their own and the up parts add on their own. The arrow from 0 to where you finish is the sum, 4 + j3. So adding complex numbers works just like adding arrows that each have an across and an up part, which textbooks call two-dimensional vectors[^4] (the Vectors course, in the Advanced maths folder, has more on them). Lay them the other way round and you finish at the same point, so the order does not matter.

Taking away is adding the opposite. Multiplying by −1 turns an arrow through 180 degrees,[^1] the same length pointing the other way. It multiplies both parts, so −(2 + j1) is −2 − j1: the across part and the up part both change sign. Then (5 + j3) − (2 + j1) = (5 + j3) + (−2 − j1) = 3 + j2: real from real, j from j. In Trigonometry you added phasors by splitting each into its floor and wall parts; a complex number is that split written as one number, and adding and taking away are easiest in this across-and-up form.[^5] **To add complex numbers, add the real parts together and the j parts together, which lays their arrows tip to tail.[^4]**

analogy.text: Think of a cable route on a drawing, measured in runs along the wall and rises up it. Run 3 m along and 1 m up, then 1 m along and 2 m up, and you end 4 m along and 3 m up from the start, whichever leg you do first. A complex sum is the same bookkeeping: the along parts add, and the up parts add.
analogy.breaks: The cable along the route is every run and rise added up, 3 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 7 m here, but the sum of two complex numbers is the straight arrow from start to finish, 5 long here, by Pythagoras. The straight distance is the legs added up only when they all point the same way.

practice.text:
- Write both numbers as a + jb with a sign in front of each part, so 4 − j1 has the j part −1.
- Add the real parts. Add the j parts. Write the answer real part first, then j part.
- To take away, change the sign of both parts of the second number, then add.
- Check on a sketch: draw the first arrow from 0 and the second from its tip, and see that the sum lands in the quarter you expect.

**Rule of thumb:** Real with real, j with j. Adding and taking away never move anything from the real part to the j part.

**Worked example:** (−3 + j2) + (4 − j5). Real parts: −3 + 4 = 1. j parts: 2 + (−5) = −3. The sum is 1 − j3. On a sketch the first arrow goes up and to the left, the second goes down and to the right from its tip, and the sum ends just right of the j axis and below the real axis. Check by taking away: (1 − j3) − (4 − j5) = (1 − j3) + (−4 + j5) = −3 + j2, the number you started with.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding everything into one number. (2 + j3) + (4 − j1) is 6 + j2, not 8.
- Losing a minus in the j part. 3 + (−1) is 2, so the answer is not 6 + j4.
- Changing only the first sign when taking away. (4 + j1) − (1 − j3) is 3 + j4, not 3 − j2.
- Plotting the parts the wrong way round. −2 + j3 is 2 left and 3 up, not 3 left and 2 up.
- Adding lengths. The sum is as long as the two arrows together only when they point the same way.
